keep: A regulator could be got round on paper. A peninsula of peat could not, and he bought 372,000 acres before he knew it was there.

lede: In 1954 a trucker who wanted a shipping line faced, by his own reckoning, a four- or five-year fight for permission. So he put the trucks in a trust and bought the ships instead.
copy: Malcolm P. McLean was president and majority stockholder of McLean Trucking Company in 1954, and he wanted to widen its reach by buying a common carrier by water. (He later spelled his first name Malcom; the 1970 court opinion on his first deal keeps the old spelling.) That needed approval from the Interstate Commerce Commission. Rail, water carrier and trucking interests all opposed the application. McLean concluded that approval might take a four- or five-year struggle, and withdrew it. His attorneys found another door. Approval would not be needed, they advised, if he gave up control of the trucking company to a management trust and bought the shipping companies' stock rather than their assets.

He did both. On 20 December 1954 he offered Waterman Steamship $3,500,000 for all the stock of two of its companies, Pan-Atlantic and Gulf Florida. At the closing on 21 January 1955 he signed the trust agreement that took the trucking company out of his control. Then the money moved. He lent Pan-Atlantic $2,500,000, which he had borrowed from Bethlehem Steel. Pan-Atlantic, on borrowed funds, paid Waterman a $2,799,820 dividend; Waterman's board took $700,180 for the stock itself. The Fifth Circuit later held that the dividend was really purchase price. Most of what Waterman received, in other words, came through the company it was selling. Levinson calls him "an entrepreneur who knew nothing about ships." On 26 April 1956 a crane at Newark lifted fifty-eight aluminum truck bodies aboard the Ideal-X, an aging tanker.

The popular account ends there, at the dock. It leaves out the second time he bought something whole before he understood it. In 1973 McLean bought 372,000 acres of North Carolina lowlands and set up First Colony Farms, meant for superfarming. He had not realised, Facing South reported in 1986, that the Pamlimarle peninsula (Pamlico and Albemarle) was blanketed with peat. So the peat became the plan. Land bought at $400 an acre would be worth $1,200 or more if the peat were removed, and in 1982 First Colony Farms and Peat Methanol Associates announced a mining project that would clear 15,000 acres of freshwater wetlands. Local fishers and farmers formed a coalition against it. Then U.S. Lines, McLean Industries and First Colony Farms filed for chapter 11 together. The court record this house has read does not say which pulled the others down. It gives the date: 24 November 1986.

bio.t: The Box: How the Shipping Container Made the World Smaller and the World Economy Bigger
bio.why: This house found no full life of McLean. This is a history of the industry with him as its central figure, and it argues that the system mattered more than the box, so read it for the man knowing he comes second.

contested: Whether McLean invented the container is the question the popular version settles fastest, and the industry's historian declines to settle it that way. Levinson's first chapter argues that the box was never the point: "A soulless aluminum or steel box" mattered for the system it made possible, not for itself. Who shipped cargo in boxes before 1956, and how much McLean took from them, is argued in Levinson's later chapters and in Cudahy's Box Boats; this house has opened neither, and names no predecessor here for that reason. The Waterman deal carries a second label. It is sometimes called an early leveraged buyout; the Fifth Circuit's question was narrower (whether $2,799,820 was a dividend or purchase price), and this house has not checked the label against a fuller record. Nor does it know whether the peat or the shipping line did more to bring the three companies into chapter 11 together.
